signals.excerpt:
Nov 25, 2026

645 output tokens/s per user at concurrency 6 on eight MI355X GPUs and 48,868 total tokens/s per GPU at concurrency 40 on four MI355X GPUs on the InferenceX AgentX workload.¹

On SemiAnalysis InferenceX's AgentX benchmark, TokenSpeed establishes a new measured throughput–interactivity frontier for Muse Spark Open on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, from latency-first serving on eight GPUs to throughput-first serving on four. The result comes from co-designing expert placement, multi-GPU communication, fused Gluon kernels and agent-aware scheduling as one serving system.¹

...

## Highlights

- A new MI355X frontier. TokenSpeed is ahead of the published baseline on both interactivity and total throughput per GPU at all six matched operating points: by 2.5–30% on interactivity and by 0.5–13% on throughput.¹
- High interactivity at low concurrency. On eight MI355X GPUs, TokenSpeed reaches 644 output tokens/s per user at concurrency 6 and 485 at concurrency 10.¹
- High throughput with more interactivity. On four GPUs at concurrency 40, TokenSpeed processes 48,868 total tokens/s per GPU at 79 output tokens/s per user, about 8% higher interactivity than the matched baseline.¹
- Optimizations span the stack. Tensor-parallel experts avoid expert token dispatch in the latency-oriented layout. Fused collectives, a persistent kernel for each eligible decode layer, and agent-aware scheduling reduce overhead across the serving path.
- Open source. AMD engineers developed these optimizations and contributed them upstream to TokenSpeed; they build on Triton/Gluon, and AMD’s open-source Iris library

Benchmark numbers in these highlights: SemiAnalysis InferenceX™, AgentX. They are SemiAnalysis’s own testing, separate from AMD internal measurements.¹

signals.title: Building a RAG System That Says "I Don't Know": Self-Correcting RAG with Llama 3.1 and LangGraph - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Abuzar Zulfiqar
Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at abuzar18.github.io • AI-assisted
# Building a RAG System That Says "I Don't Know": Self-Correcting RAG with Llama 3.1 and LangGraph
Most RAG demos have the same flaw: ask them something the documents never mention, and they answer anyway, confidently and wrongly. In a demo that is a curiosity. In production it is how a support bot invents a refund policy.
I built Llama Agentic RAG around the opposite rule: **an answer must be supported by cited sources, or the system says "I don't know."** It runs fully locally on Llama 3.1 8B through Ollama, which fits in 8 GB of VRAM, so private documents never leave the machine.
This post walks through the design and the choices that made it work on a small model.
## The workflow
The pipeline is a LangGraph state machine with five stages:
1. **Retrieve** the top-k chunks from a vector index. Every chunk has a stable id such as `handbook.md#3`, so citations stay traceable.
2. **Grade** each chunk for relevance with the LLM before anything is generated. Off-topic context never reaches the answer.
3. **Rewrite** the query once if no chunk is relevant. Vague questions often recover here; if they don't, the graph refuses.
4. **Generate** an answer only from the numbered context, citing `[n]` after each claim.
5. **Check groundedness**: a judge prompt verifies the answer against the context. An unsupported answer is replaced by a refusal.
The key idea is that hallucinations become refusals, not wrong answers. A refusal is annoying; a confident wrong answer is expensive.
## Making it work on an 8B model
Large models forgive sloppy prompts. Small models don't, so a few details mattered more than any framework choice:
* **One-word verdicts.** Llama 3.1 8B is unreliable with complex JSON schemas, so the grading and groundedness prompts ask for `yes` or `no`, and parsing is tolerant of extra words.
* **Strip reasoning tags.** If you swap in a reasoning model, its ` ` blocks are removed before parsing.
* **Citations are enforced, not requested.** An answer without valid `[n]` citations is treated as ungrounded, even if it sounds right.
* **Config over code.** Every model, path and threshold is an environment variable, so trying another Ollama model is a one-line change.
## Measure the refusals
A RAG system that never says "I don't know" isn't production-ready, so the evaluation set deliberately includes unanswerable questions. The harness reports:
|Metric|What it tells you|
|Retrieval hit rate|Did we retrieve an expected source for answerable questions?|
|Citation precision|Do cited chunks come from expected sources?|
|Refusal accuracy|Were unanswerable questions correctly refused?|
|False-refusal rate|Were answerable questions wrongly refused?|
|Judge correctness|LLM-as-judge score against a reference answer|
|p50 / p95 latency|What does it cost the user in time?|
Refusal accuracy and false-refusal rate pull against each other, which is exactly why you need both. Tighten the groundedness check and refusals get safer while false refusals rise. The numbers make that trade-off visible instead of a matter of opinion.
Treat prompt and model changes like code changes: they ship only if the evals hold.
## Tests that don't need a GPU
CI runs the full graph with scripted fake LLM replies and deterministic embeddings. That covers the happy path, query rewrite, refusal, ungrounded answers, missing citations and reasoning-tag stripping, all without a model or a GPU. It is the cheapest way to keep a graph's control flow honest as it grows.
## Use it from Claude with MCP
The same graph is exposed as an MCP tool, `ask\_documents`, so Claude Desktop, Claude Code or any MCP client can query your documents and get cited answers back. The FastAPI service exposes `/ask`, `/ingest` and `/health` for everything else.
## What's next
The roadmap is the usual path from reference to production: hybrid retrieval with BM25 and a cross-encoder reranker, a persistent vector database such as pgvector or Qdrant, tracing with Langfuse, streaming, and PDF and DOCX ingestion.
The code is MIT-licensed: github.com/abuzar18/llama-agentic-rag. If you are building RAG for a team that can't afford confident wrong answers, I'd be glad to compare notes.

signals.title: How to Optimize NVFP4 Attention on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell Through Register Recycling | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Attention can be a major bottleneck when serving world foundation models, where long sequences make inference computationally demanding. On NVIDIA Hopper and NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs, FlashAttention3 and FlashAttention4 improve attention performance by overlapping matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA) operations through softmax within a thread block.

However, these hardware-specific pipelines cannot be applied directly to the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series (SM120), which uses a different Tensor Core architecture. For video generation models using BF16 inference, attention remains primarily MMA-bound on NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPUs, while softmax is a major bottleneck in forward attention on Blackwell data center GPUs.

Introduced with NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, NVFP4 offers hardware-accelerated 4-bit matrix multiplication, enabling higher Tensor Core throughput and creating an opportunity to accelerate attention beyond BF16. But sustaining high throughput requires careful coordination of softmax, data movement, and intermediate storage. Dependencies between these stages can leave Tensor Cores idle, limiting how effectively the kernel uses the available compute.

This post explains how to accelerate NVFP4 attention on the SM120 architecture through register recycling and improved scheduling. By reclaiming score registers after the softmax outputs have been packed into NVFP4, the next tile’s matrix multiplication can overlap with remaining softmax work on the current tile. This creates a more efficient pipeline that reduces Tensor Core idle time and improves utilization without requiring a second full score buffer.

Reactor, a developer platform that provides global low-latency infrastructure and APIs for deploying and scaling real-time video, robotics, and world models, integrated this kernel in their production serving stack to serve real customer traffic and saw tremendous speedups. Their benchmarks are shared in this post.

...

...

Reactor evaluated the optimized kernel on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU with 96 GB of memory (SM120), measuring its impact across four world-model workloads.

### Attention kernel speedup

To isolate the scheduling optimization, the original and optimized NVFP4 kernels were compared using identical 

 inputs, packed tensors, and `log-sum-exp` settings.

| Workload / mask | Original (ms) | Optimized (ms) | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LongLive 7,040 / noncausal | 0.75052 | 0.63548 | 1.18x |
| LongLive 7,040 / causal | 0.44992 | 0.37927 | 1.19x |
| Synthetic 4,096 / noncausal | 0.28962 | 0.23190 | 1.25x |
| Synthetic 4,096 / causal | 0.21199 | 0.16087 | 1.32x |
| Synthetic 8,192 / noncausal | 1.00177 | 0.85648 | 1.17x |
| Synthetic 8,192 / causal | 0.76466 | 0.46659 | 1.64x |
| Synthetic 16,384 / noncausal | 3.80862 | 3.25377 | 1.17x |
| Synthetic 16,384 / causal | 2.20630 | 1.78152 | 1.24x |

Table 1. Core NVFP4 latency before and after optimization on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell

All cases use batch size 1, 24 heads, head dimension 128, and equal query/key lengths. The 7,040-token input was captured from LongLive; the other inputs are synthetic. Core timing excludes Q/K/V quantization and output-stride restoration

Measurements used three fresh processes per implementation, alternating run order, active prewarming, and repeated CUDA-event timing blocks.

Reactor integrated this NVFP4 attention kernel into its production serving infrastructure and used it to serve real customer traffic across several models. Table 2 shows the impact on end-to-end model inference latency on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.

Latency was measured for the complete model path per video chunk, full generation, or action prediction. For the video-chunk and action-prediction benchmarks, the BF16 baseline uses native cuDNN attention. Timings include quantization, layout conversion, and decoded CPU-frame or action output, but exclude model loading, warmup, networking, queueing, and client pacing.

signals.title: Nvidia Cosmos 3 Nano on RTX 5070: 12GB VRAM Benchmarks - TechRepublic
signals.excerpt:
On Nov. 24, Nvidia published a new memory-offloading technique that allows Cosmos 3 Nano to run on GPUs with as little as 12GB of VRAM, including the RTX 5070. The method moves model weights between system RAM and the GPU instead of keeping everything in graphics memory.

...

According to Nvidia’s technical report, its new adapter builds on Hugging Face Diffusers’ group-offloading technology.

Instead of loading all model weights onto the GPU simultaneously, the system keeps inactive weights in regular system RAM.

When a particular transformer block is needed, the adapter transfers it to the graphics card, performs the calculations, and makes room for the next block.

This reduces peak VRAM consumption without shrinking the underlying model.

The system also manages memory during video decoding and safety checks.

The catch is that system RAM and VRAM are not interchangeable. Moving model weights repeatedly creates additional data transfers and can increase processing time.

Nvidia says the method isn’t designed for interactive, real-time generation.

The company tested four consumer GPUs:

- RTX 5070: 12GB VRAM
- RTX 5080: 16GB VRAM
- RTX 4090: 24GB VRAM
- RTX 5090: 32GB VRAM

All four systems had approximately 128GB of system RAM.

Nvidia emphasizes that 128GB describes its benchmark machines, not a confirmed minimum requirement. Systems with less RAM may work, but the published tests don’t establish how much memory they need or how quickly they will perform.

...

The RTX 5070 results give developers a practical idea of the compromises involved.

Nvidia tested text-to-video generation using a 189-frame workload at 24 frames per second, producing approximately 7.9 seconds of video.

The company measured both generation time and peak GPU memory consumption across three resolutions.

RTX 5070 results using BF16 precision:

- 720p (1280 × 720): 43.75 minutes, using 9.94 GiB of GPU memory.
- 480p (848 × 480): 14.16 minutes, using 6.68 GiB.
- 240p (432 × 240): 3.46 minutes, using 4.30 GiB.

The difference is considerable.

Reducing output resolution from 720p to 240p shortened the generation time from nearly 44 minutes to less than four minutes.

For developers testing prompts, motion, or scene composition, starting at a lower resolution could save substantial time.

What happens when Nvidia uses FP8?

Nvidia also tested a checkpoint using mixed FP8 and BF16 precision.

FP8 stores some model data in a more compact format, reducing memory requirements. However, attention operations still use BF16, so the entire pipeline isn’t operating in FP8.

On the RTX 5070, Nvidia reported:

- 720p: 37.26 minutes, using 9.16 GiB.
- 480p: 11.94 minutes, using 6.23 GiB.
- 240p: 2.84 minutes, using 3.95 GiB.

At 720p, the FP8 configuration completed the workload approximately 15% faster than the BF16 version.

However, these are single-run vendor benchmarks rather than repeated independent tests.

The reported durations also exclude initial model loading and video-file encoding. Actual time from launching a workload to obtaining a finished MP4 file may therefore be longer.

signals.title: PrismML shrinks a 54 GB language model to 5.9 GB by reducing every weight to just three possible values
signals.excerpt:
Startup PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an updated version of its aggressively compressed language model. It's based on Qwen3.8-27B and takes up just 5.9 GB of memory, same as its predecessor. That's possible because of ternary quantization, where each weight can only be one of three values (−1, 0, or +1) instead of the usual 16-bit storage. At full precision, a model this size would need about 54 GB.

Bonsai 2.5 is designed to perform more reliably on agentic tasks that involve long chains of tool calls. It needs fewer passes and tokens than Bonsai 2, and it's less likely to get stuck in loops or spiral into drawn-out reasoning phases.

The benchmark numbers reflect the improvement. On SWE-bench Verified, the score jumps from 60.8 to 75.6 percent. The full Qwen model hits 80.6. On AppWorld, an agent benchmark, Bonsai leaps from 51.2 to 90.5, landing just behind the base model. On LiveCodeBench v6, the new version scores slightly lower than its predecessor.

On an RTX 4090, the model generates about 204 tokens per second using multi-token prediction. The weights are available under an Apache 2.0 license and run via llama.cpp on Nvidia and Intel GPUs, as well as through MLX on Mac, iPhone, and iPad.

signals.title: Databricks open-sources Omnigent meta-harness for governing coding…
signals.excerpt:
| November 26, 2026| By LDS Team

...

Databricks has open-sourced Omnigent under Apache 2.0, a meta-harness that sits above agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pi. According to the company, it lets teams swap or combine harnesses with one-line changes, enforce policies such as cost budgets outside the prompt, and share live agent sessions by URL.

Databricks has open-sourced Omnigent under the Apache 2.0 license. Omnigent is a meta-harness: a layer above agent harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex, Pi and custom agents. The company says it is meant to compose, govern and share agents from one place.

### What Omnigent adds

According to the Databricks announcement, each harness only understands its own sessions, which makes combining or swapping them difficult. Omnigent adds a common API that wraps terminal-based agents (Claude Code, Codex, Pi) and SDKs (OpenAI Agents, Claude Agents SDK). The company's stated insight is that every harness presents the same interface to users: messages and files in, text streams and tool calls out.

The project's site describes an architecture with two parts. A runner wraps any agent in a uniform session. A server adds policies and shared history, and exposes each session over the terminal, web, a native app, mobile and a REST API.

### Omnigent at a glance

- • Composition: switch between Claude Code, Codex, Pi and your own agents with one-line changes.
- • Control: stateful policies such as cost budgets and permissions, enforced at the meta-harness layer rather than via prompts.
- • Collaboration: share live sessions via URL with full history, so teammates can review, comment and steer together.
- • Sandboxes: run agents in a local OS sandbox or a remote cloud sandbox; Databricks names Modal and Daytona as hosted providers.
- • Built-in agents: Polly, a coding orchestrator, and Debby, a model debate; custom agents are defined in YAML.
- • License: Apache 2.0.

### Policies and sandboxing

The project's site lists stateful spend caps, model routing and risk-based escalation as contextual policies. On Linux and macOS, it says sandboxes can restrict filesystem and network access and broker credentials without exposing them to the agent.

Because the policies sit outside the prompt, a budget or access rule does not depend on which harness is running. That follows from the design the company describes. It matters for teams that run several coding agents at once and want one set of limits.

...

### Open questions

The announcement and project site give no benchmarks, overhead figures or pricing beyond the open-source license. They do not detail how deeply policies can inspect actions inside a third-party harness. Teams will need to test those limits and the stability of a new project before relying on it for governance.

signals.title: JetBrains' latest Mellum coding model uses 45% fewer tokens. It got there by not thinking. - The New Stack
signals.excerpt:
JetBrains has launched a new variant of its open source coding model, one designed to tackle quick code edits, tool calls and all the smaller tasks that AI coding agents perform in the course of solving bigger problems.

Mellum2.1 Instruct, as it’s called, is the latest installment in JetBrains’ in-house coding model lineup. The original Mellum, which debuted back in 2024, was a proprietary model built specifically for low-latency code completion in JetBrains’ IDEs. 

Then in June this year, JetBrains introduced Mellum2, a more versatile, 12-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model released under an Apache 2.0 license in both reasoning (Thinking) and non-reasoning (Instruct) variants. While Mellum2 was trained to handle individual coding tasks and tool calls, the next iteration would focus more specifically on how agents operate across entire code repositories.

That came last month with Mellum2.1 Thinking, which retained the same underlying architecture as Mellum2, but with an additional stage of reinforcement learning (RL) in which the model learned to navigate repositories, use shell and file tools, and make changes that would pass hidden tests.

With Mellum2.1 Instruct, JetBrains is now extending that same repository-level training to its non-reasoning model, which generates answers without an explicit chain-of-thought. As with its Thinking sibling, the company used Nvidia’s open source NeMo RL and NeMo Megatron-Bridge libraries to train the model using infrastructure capable of running 10,000 sandboxes concurrently.

The result is a leaner coding model fine-tuned for speed and token efficiency, capable of handling many of the same agentic tasks as its Thinking counterpart, with about half the token consumption, according to JetBrains’ testing.

...

In its own benchmarking, JetBrains pits Mellum2.1 Instruct against the previous Mellum2 Instruct model, as well as Alibaba’s Qwen3.5 9B and Google’s Gemma 4 E4B, with reasoning disabled in both competing models. The six benchmarks cover agentic coding, multilingual code generation, tool use, instruction following and mathematical problem-solving.

Mellum2.1 Instruct doubled its predecessor’s score on SWE-bench Verified, which measures a model’s ability to resolve real-world software issues, jumping from 20.2% to 40.4%. It also outperformed all three models on the MultiPL-E code generation benchmark and broadly matched Qwen3.5 9B on ToolHop, which evaluates multi-step tool use.

Mellum2.1 Instruct: Comparative benchmark performance

Qwen3.5 9B, it’s worth noting, still came out ahead on SWE-bench Verified, scoring 49.8%. However, JetBrains points to Mellum’s MoE architecture, which activates just 2.5 billion of its 12 billion parameters for each token. According to the company’s earlier testing, this enables Mellum2.1 to generate tokens around 1.4 times as fast as Qwen3.5 9B for individual requests and 1.8 times as fast under load.

Perhaps more pertinent to this particular release, though, is how Mellum2.1 Instruct compares with its Thinking sibling in terms of token generation. In JetBrains’ agentic coding tests, the new model generated an average of 5,600 tokens per task, compared with 10,100 for Thinking — a reduction of 45%.

When tokens associated with tool calls were excluded, that reduction rose to 73%.

...

There are trade-offs, of course. While the two variants perform almost equally well on SWE-bench Verified, the gap widens on benchmarks that draw on competitive programming and mathematics competitions.

“On hard algorithmic and math problems, such as those in LiveCodeBench and AIME, thinking is crucial, and so Mellum2.1 Thinking remains the better choice,” Ingman writes.

...

Mellum2.1 Instruct is available on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license, including a GGUF version for running the model locally on hardware with limited memory. JetBrains is also releasing a multi-token prediction (MTP) head alongside the model, which predicts multiple tokens ahead to accelerate generation by up to 1.8 times, according to the company.

signals.title: Open Software Package Behind Ollama and LM Studio Gets 1.0 Release
signals.excerpt:
Published Nov 27, 2026

llama.cpp, an open source software package that helps users run AI language models locally, finally reached version 1.0 after more than three years in development. The milestone signals that its developers consider it mature and stable enough for a major release.

What’s new: The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face released version 1.0.0 of llama.cpp and of ggml, the library that performs its underlying math. The release shows that llama.cpp is still widely used and under active development, and that local AI is arguably more popular than ever. The new package adds support for several new models, including Kimi-K3.1 Pro, a text-to-speech feature for its built-in server, and a redesigned chat interface.

How it works: Georgi Gerganov started llama.cpp in March 2023, about a week after Meta’s first LLaMA language model leaked online. Gerganov wrote it as a plain C/C++ program, compiled to run directly on a computer’s processor. Meta’s own code for running LLaMA required Python, the PyTorch framework, CUDA, and an Nvidia graphics chip. Gerganov’s version had no dependencies and could run on a MacBook or any other machine, regardless of whether it had a specific GPU. Llama.cpp has been in use ever since, powering apps like Ollama and LM Studio that likewise help run local AI models on ordinary machines.

- While it’s perhaps best known for running AI models on laptops, llama.cpp can perform inference on hardware that ranges from servers to edge machines. The project supports “more than 150 architecture variants,” the team says.
- llama.cpp loads models stored in GGUF, a file format designed to load quickly. Hugging Face hosts thousands of models compatible with llama.cpp.
- The software relies heavily on quantization, which shrinks a model by storing its weights (the numbers that encode what it learned) at lower precision, for instance as 4-bit instead of 32-bit numbers. Quantized models require less memory and often run faster, sometimes at a cost in accuracy.
- The ggml library interacts with different kinds of hardware through separate backends, modules written for specific chips or programming standards. These include CUDA for Nvidia GPUs, Metal for Apple chips, and the cross-vendor Vulkan standard, as well as backends for ordinary CPUs.
- A bundled server accepts requests in formats modeled on OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s APIs, so many apps written for cloud models can use a local model instead. The project makes “no strong claims of compatibility” with OpenAI’s specification but says the server “suffices to support many apps.”

signals.title: MixMoMo Tests 80-Billion-Parameter Generative AI on Smartphones Using Both GPU and NPU | Joho no Todai
signals.excerpt:
Researchers have demonstrated large generative AI models on smartphones with 16GB of memory. MixMoMo adjusts weight-quantization precision based on the input and distributes computation between the GPU and NPU to balance response quality with generation speed.

Key points

- Research target: MixMoMo is an inference system for large MoE models on smartphones that loads and runs the weights of the required experts.
- Precision control: It chooses the precision for each expert using the input at inference time and a premeasured estimate of the effect of quantization.
- Computation split: It estimates GPU and NPU execution times to distribute work and also parallelizes dequantization inside the NPU.
- What the performance means: MixMoMo shows that evaluating generative AI speed on smartphones requires looking at total execution time, including data loading and conversion.

## How can a smartphone with 16GB run such a large AI model?

Researchers from Peking University and Tianjin University in China have published a paper on MixMoMo, a generative AI inference system for smartphones. The original title is MixMoMo: Accelerating Extra–Large MoE Inference with Mixed–Precision GPU–NPU Execution on Mobile Devices.

The OnePlus 15 used in the experiments had a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 16GB of memory, and 256GB of UFS 4.1 storage. The OnePlus 13 system used a Snapdragon 8 Elite, 24GB of memory, and 1TB of UFS 4.0 storage.

The three AI models tested were Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B has 80 billion total parameters, but its developer's specifications say only 3 billion parameters are active during inference.

This is possible because of a design called mixture of experts (MoE), which selects the necessary computational components, or experts, from multiple components in the model according to the input. A Qwen3-Next MoE layer uses 10 of 512 available experts.

As the total number of parameters grows, so does the storage capacity needed for the weights—the numerical values learned during training. But loading the selected experts' weights from storage into memory as needed makes it possible to perform inference with limited memory.

In fact, BigMoMo, earlier research involving some of the same researchers, reported running MoE models with up to 80 billion parameters on mobile devices. MixMoMo improves both the precision used when loading model weights and the computations performed with those weights.

...

## Where precision can be reduced depends on the input

Quantization, which represents model weights with fewer bits, is used to reduce storage and memory consumption. Lowering precision reduces capacity requirements, but it can also affect the AI's answers.

The team found that quantization can substantially change the model's final output even when an expert receives only a small weight in the combined output. The effect on the final output varies with the combination of quantization errors in the weights and the data entering the expert.

MixMoMo measures the effect of quantizing each expert on the final output in advance. During actual inference, it combines the incoming data values with those premeasured results to estimate the risk of reducing precision.

The available precisions are nominally 2-bit, 4-bit, 8-bit, and FP16, or 16-bit floating point. MixMoMo begins by assigning low precision, then raises the precision of the necessary experts until the estimated risk falls within an acceptable range. Its distinguishing feature is that it selects precision according to the input.

Weights at different precisions use a common representation in storage and are loaded at the precision required for inference. This design also limits the additional storage capacity that would otherwise result from using multiple precisions.

## Reducing GPU and NPU wait times

GPUs and NPUs, processors specialized for AI operations, differ in the calculations and data handling they perform well. In the team's comparison, simply assigning experts according to the processing capacity of each processor could be slower than using the NPU alone for some combinations of quantization precision.

When both processors calculate in parallel, combining the results requires waiting for the slower one to finish.

MixMoMo therefore measures GPU and NPU execution times in advance for different precisions and numbers of experts. It accounts for loading weights, converting them into the format needed for computation, performing the calculation, and transferring data, then chooses the split predicted to complete expert processing in the shortest time during inference.

The researchers also modified processing inside the NPU. On the tested GPU, low-precision weights can be unpacked and dequantized—converted into the numerical values used for computation—with the matrix calculation combined into a single operation. On the tested NPU, quantized weights are converted to FP16 before matrix calculations are performed.

Previously, each divided block of weights required preparation for unpacking and dequantization. MixMoMo processes compatible blocks together to use the NPU's parallel-computing capability. It also groups work by precision at each computation stage, reducing the overhead from execution commands and synchronization on the NPU.

The implementation uses the existing generative AI inference engine llama.cpp. The team added about 8,000 lines of C/C++ code for OpenCL, Qualcomm's Hexagon HTP, and other components.

## What contributed to the speedup?

The researchers compared performance on five types of datasets: math problems, code generation, news summarization, knowledge questions, and dialogue. All mixed-precision methods used an average expert quantization precision of 4 bits, and the team measured processing time per output token, the unit into which text is divided for processing.

MixMoMo Smartphone Performance Evaluation

| Generation-speed comparison with existing methods (two devices, five tasks; mixed precision averages 4 bits) | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AI model | | Vs. uniform 4-bit | Vs. best mixed-precision method |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B | | 3.61x | 1.50x |
| Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B | | 4.06x | 1.61x |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | | 3.49x | 1.48x |
| Three-model average | | 3.72x | 1.53x |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B: Added Features and Generation Speed | | | |
| Added features (cumulative) | | GSM8K ms/token | Three-task average |
| Uniform 4-bit (baseline) | | 1111.11 | 1.00x |
| + Quantization-precision control | | 1123.59 | 1.01x |
| + GPU-NPU distribution | | 498.26 | 2.32x |
| + Parallel NPU dequantization and processing integration | | 327.87 | 3.61x |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B: Answer Quality | | | |
| Method | GSM8K accuracy | HumanEval Pass@1 | MMLU-Pro Accuracy |
| FP16 | 84.53% | 92.12% | 76.35% |
| Uniform 4-bit | 80.46% | 87.94% | 71.48% |
| MixMoMo | 84.48% | 92.00% | 75.87% |

The paper reports an average token-generation speed across the three models that was 3.72x that of uniform 4-bit quantization (Q4_0). It was an average of 1.53x the fastest existing mixed-precision method for each model. Compared with uniform 4-bit quantization, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B was 3.61x faster, Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B was 4.06x faster, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B was 3.49x faster.

For Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, the team also conducted tests on three tasks while adding each feature in stages. Adding only quantization-precision control produced an average speed of 1.01x that of uniform 4-bit quantization. Adding GPU-NPU work distribution raised it to 2.32x, while also adding parallel NPU dequantization and integration of processing by precision brought it to 3.61x.

On GSM8K, a benchmark of mathematical word problems, uniform 4-bit quantization required 1,111.11 milliseconds per output token, while MixMoMo with all features enabled required 327.87 milliseconds. That is an improvement from about 0.90 tokens per second to about 3.05 tokens per second.

The researchers also measured answer quality for MixMoMo with quantization-precision control. On GSM8K, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B achieved 84.53% accuracy with FP16, 80.46% with uniform 4-bit quantization, and 84.48% with MixMoMo. On HumanEval, a set of programming tasks used to assess code generation, Pass@1—the probability that a single generated answer passes the tests—was 92.12% for FP16, 87.94% for uniform 4-bit quantization, and 92.00% for MixMoMo.

The quality comparison and staged speed measurements show that precision control and acceleration play different roles. Varying precision limits quality degradation from quantization, while improving data preparation and computation assignment increases speed. The research is notable for combining the effects of both approaches.

signals.title: DFly2: Tencent's open drafter speeds up long contexts | Neural Daily
signals.excerpt:
## What happened

On November 26, Tencent's Hunyuan AI Infra team fully open-sourced DFly2: the weights, the training code in its AngelSpec framework, and the technical report (arXiv, GitHub). DFly2 is a block-parallel drafter for speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes several tokens, and the large model verifies them in one pass. It is lossless: same output, just faster.

New MoE drafters are available for Hy4 flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash (Hugging Face). Hy4 and Hy4 flash already ship with this drafter. Our coverage of Hy4's open weights: Tencent Hy4 open weights are out: 770B MoE, 49B active.

## What is new

Models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 use native sparse attention: in each layer, a trained indexer picks a fixed number of positions from the context, and the KV cache is stored compressed. Today's drafters, however, were built for dense models. They keep their own cache over the whole prompt or a sliding window. The report says DFlash's own cache adds a fifth to the per-token KV on Hy4 flash and three quarters on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

DFly2's idea is simple: the sparse target has already decided where to look, and paid for it. So each draft layer:

- reads the KV cache of its paired target layer (KV sharing),
- at exactly the positions that layer's indexer selected (Index sharing),
- starts from that layer's weights and also receives the target's last-layer hidden state.

There is no separate cache, no scoring pass, and no role in prefill. According to the README, each draft token attends to at most about 2,000 keys regardless of context length. The report also measured that a selection made one step early still covers close to nine tenths of what later tokens select on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

## The numbers

The team compared DFly2 with DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe. On all three targets and every benchmark, DFly2 accepted more tokens per step. Its margin over the stronger baseline is 3.9% to 10.5% on general workloads and 10.0% to 31.5% on long-context and agentic workloads up to 128K.

Tencent · Press kit · Source

Source: Tencent, AngelSpec README

- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at high concurrency and matched per-user decode speed, 64K context: 62% more throughput on long-context sets and 81% more on agentic sets.
- Hy4 flash, agentic average: 3.41x decoding and 1.67x end-to-end speedup over autoregressive decoding (greedy, single request).
- Hy4 flash and Hy4 on agentlongbench 64K: 4.20x decoding speedup.

Caveats: these are Tencent's own measurements, with no independent benchmark yet. The 4.20x figure is the best case, and end-to-end gains are much smaller. Each drafter is tied to its target model and must be retrained for others.

signals.title: 10 Open-Source AI Agent Frameworks Compared for Production Use - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Posted on Nov 26 

# 10 Open-Source AI Agent Frameworks Compared for Production Use 

An AI agent is a program that uses a large language model (LLM) to plan, call tools, and complete a multi-step task. Those tools might look up data, send an email, or create a ticket. Most engineering teams start with an open-source framework instead of writing everything from scratch.

This article highlights 10 notable AI agent frameworks on GitHub, with figures collected on November 20, 2026, their licenses, and suggestions on which to choose.

## At a glance 

| # | Repository | GitHub stars | Language | License | Best fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | langgenius/dify | ~161.5k | Python, TypeScript | Apache 2.0-based with additional terms | Building agents with a visual editor and minimal code |
| 2 | langchain-ai/langchain | ~149.9k | Python | MIT | A large ecosystem with many integrations |
| 3 | crewAIInc/crewAI | ~61.1k | Python | MIT | Multiple agents collaborating in defined roles |
| 4 | run-llama/llama_index | ~53.0k | Python | MIT | Document-based agents and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) |
| 5 | langchain-ai/langgraph | ~45.2k | Python | MIT | Multi-step workflows that need explicit control |
| 6 | agno-agi/agno | ~43.2k | Python | Apache 2.0 | Lightweight agents with built-in memory |
| 7 | openai/openai-agents-python | ~30.8k | Python | MIT | Getting started quickly and handing work between agents |
| 8 | huggingface/smolagents | ~30.5k | Python | Apache 2.0 | Minimal agents that can express actions in code |
| 9 | mastra-ai/mastra | ~29.7k | TypeScript | Apache 2.0 except for enterprise components under ee/ | TypeScript and Node.js teams |
| 10 | google/adk-python | ~22.3k | Python | Apache 2.0 | Teams working with Gemini and Google Cloud |

The original article reports rounded GitHub API counts from November 20, 2026. Stars measure attention and should be considered alongside maintenance, documentation, and licensing.

## How we selected the projects 

- Maintenance. The original selection looked for commits in November 2026 and excluded repositories marked as archived at the time of review.
- Business use. The selection favored software that could be used internally and highlighted additional commercial terms.
- Community. The projects had more than 20,000 stars at the time of the snapshot. Contributor activity and documentation were also considered.
- Variety. The shortlist includes visual tools, code-first libraries, and options for Python and TypeScript teams.

## 1. Dify: Build agents in a visual editor 

Dify provides a web interface for building chatbots, agents, and RAG workflows. Choose a model, add documents, arrange the steps in a workflow, and expose the result through an API or chat page.

Screenshot of the Dify repository, captured November 24, 2026.

- Strengths. Quick to prototype, with support for multiple model providers, document management, conversation history, and logs.
- License considerations. Dify uses Apache 2.0-based terms with additional conditions covering multi-tenant services and removal of branding or copyright information from the interface. Internal use within one company may fit the base terms. Review the terms for your actual deployment.
- Best fit. Businesses that want to test an internal assistant on their own documents.

## 2. LangChain: A broad integration ecosystem 

LangChain connects LLMs to tools and data. It has integrations for many popular models, vector databases, and APIs.

...

Many examples and integrations, with a large community of practitioners.
- Trade-off. The abstraction layers may add overhead to a small project. For a multi-step agent that needs finer control, see LangGraph in section 5.
- License. MIT.

...

## 4. LlamaIndex: Agents that work with documents 

LlamaIndex excels at reading, chunking, indexing, and querying documents such as PDFs, Word files, and spreadsheets. The repository describes it as a document processing platform for AI.

- Best fit. Assistants that answer questions from company policies, contracts, and product records, or look up legal documents internally.
- License. MIT.

## 5. LangGraph: Explicit control over each step 

LangGraph, from the LangChain team, defines workflows as graphs. Nodes represent steps, and edges determine where execution goes next. The workflow can persist state, pause for human approval, and resume afterward.

- Best fit. Workflows that need human approval before writing data, such as approving a quotation or expense.
- License. MIT.

signals.title: NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin Leads MLPerf Training and Agentic Inference Tests
signals.excerpt:
The company says Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered the fastest training time on six of seven MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmarks and was the only platform with submissions across the full suite. In the new MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 tests, NVIDIA reported more than 10 times the throughput per kilowatt of a GB300 NVL72 configuration on one agentic workload at a shared responsiveness target.

...

The MLPerf Training v6.1 suite spans language models, image generation, recommendation systems and reinforcement-learning post-training. NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 completed all seven benchmarks. It led six of them, while a 10,240-GPU NVIDIA GB300 deployment produced the fastest absolute result on the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark.

On the 671-billion-parameter DeepSeek-V3 mixture-of-experts test, Vera Rubin trained the model in 4.14 minutes on 1,024 GPUs, compared with 8.03 minutes for GB300 at the same GPU count, according to NVIDIA’s presentation of the MLPerf data. At the larger 10,240-GPU scale, GB300 completed the workload in 1.38 minutes, showing that the older platform still has a role in very large cluster deployments.

Vera Rubin also led the new Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO reinforcement-learning post-training test. NVIDIA reported a 10.44-minute result at 1,024 GPUs, compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300. The company submitted the workload using both TensorRT-LLM and vLLM inference backends, with the latter recording 10.94 minutes.

...

The companion MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 submission measures a different problem: how many users and agentic tasks a system can serve while maintaining acceptable response speed. The tests use coding and enterprise workflows, with generated tool calls and workflow intent checked against reference values. Separate SWE-bench Verified evaluations are intended to assess end-to-end task solving.

NVIDIA reported that Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered more than 10 times the throughput per kilowatt of GB300 NVL72 for Kimi K3 at a shared minimum end-to-end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user. The comparison used 32 Vera Rubin accelerators against 48 GB300 accelerators. NVIDIA’s developer documentation says Vera Rubin also achieved five to 10 times higher throughput per kilowatt across Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, while producing three to five times higher interactivity at matched concurrency.

The reported gains are not attributed to hardware alone. NVIDIA says the platform combines HBM4 memory, Tensor Cores and sixth-generation NVLink with serving techniques such as prefix caching, state reuse and NVIDIA Dynamo routing. These methods attempt to avoid recomputing shared context and to balance the different demands of prompt processing and token generation.

...

## Evidence, comparisons and remaining caveats

The MLPerf Training results are based on entries published by MLCommons, while NVIDIA’s technical posts interpret the results and highlight its own systems. NVIDIA says 20 organizations submitted Training results using its platforms, including cloud providers, server makers and research institutions. That demonstrates ecosystem participation, but it should not be read as an independent measure of customer adoption or production deployment.

The Endpoints comparison requires more caution. The GB300 result cited by NVIDIA was verified by the MLCommons Association, while the Vera Rubin result was listed as provisional and pending verification and peer review. The figures can therefore change. The comparison also uses different accelerator counts and operating-power configurations, and the headline ratio is calculated at a shared response-speed threshold rather than under identical concurrency.

NVIDIA’s training material additionally references unverified reruns using a newer software stack that improved results on several workloads. Those reruns may indicate continuing optimization, but they are not equivalent to finalized benchmark submissions. Similarly, claims that Vera Rubin is generally available through cloud infrastructure partners are supplied by NVIDIA and do not establish how broadly customers can access the systems, at what prices or under what capacity constraints.

The most defensible conclusion is narrower: Vera Rubin has shown strong early results in a recognized benchmark suite, with particularly large gains on workloads involving model scale, communication and agentic serving. The results do not by themselves establish total cost of ownership, reliability in production or superiority across every customer workload.

signals.excerpt:
November 26, 2026 November 27, 2026 | Sarita Chebbi 

What if you could build software using AI agents without paying for expensive subscriptions or sending your code to the cloud? Prof. Karthik Vaidyanathan and his team is working towards making this possible with AutoSE, a Made-in-India, patent-pending, open-source, locally deployable agentic harness/tool that aims to make AI-powered software development more accessible, private and sustainable.

...

Karthik Vaidyanathan and his students at the Software Engineering Research Centre (SERC), IIIT Hyderabad definitely believe so and are demonstrating this with AutoSE (Autonomous Software Engineering), an open-source tool that allows AI agents to build software locally, using smaller language models.

...

The Trappings Of An Agent To understand AutoSE, the professor remarks that it’s essential to understand the difference between an AI model and an AI agent. “Models like LLMs have become extremely popular. They take an input like a prompt and generate code for you. But that’s where they stop; they can only generate code,” he says, adding that building software requires more capabilities than mere code generation. This is where an agentic harness comes in providing the whole shebang of tools, memory, prompts and mechanisms for planning and evaluating tasks, enabling a model to perform more complex activities. The central idea behind this was to create an ecosystem around these models that would enable them to undertake software development while keeping everything local. “There are a lot of open-source models available that can be hosted on an organization’s own infrastructure, but they lack a ‘harness’ that can work around these models,” explains Prof. Vaidyanathan.

...

Vaidyanathan as explanation for having an open-source version. It is available under the Apache 2.0 licence, which means individuals, developers, students and institutions can download and use it without paying for the harness itself. “All they need is a reasonably capable machine and a suitable locally hosted model.”

...

However, they have ... The researchers explain that simply replacing a large model in an existing AI coding tool with a smaller one does not necessarily work. ... They found that while these combinations performed very well with powerful models, their performance dropped dramatically when smaller models were introduced.

...

For instance, SLMs may not anticipate that a software package needs to be installed within a virtual environment. A larger model might automatically recognise this requirement, while a smaller one may simply attempt the installation and encounter an error. AutoSE addresses such limitations through mechanisms such as memory, structured planning and architectural records. The system can retain information about previous actions, remember what worked and use that information to guide subsequent tasks. The team is working on improving this memory mechanism. The objective is to ensure that an agent working on a large codebase does not repeatedly ask for the same information or make the same mistakes. They are also exploring ways to select and switch between smaller models depending on the task to make them more efficient.
